newsitem.title: CHINA: China to restructure state assets in 1997.
newsitem.headline: China to restructure state assets in 1997.

text.p: China plans to strengthen the management of state assets in 1997 to try to curb a drain of state property and to improve the quality of its remaining assets, state media said on Tuesday.

China, where the state and government have long held a virtual monopoly of assets, must develop a property rights transfer market and standardise property rights transfers, state media quoted Vice Minister of Finance Zhang Youcai as telling a national conference.
"Besides government guidance, we should fully tap the role of the market in issues concerning the mergers, auction, leasing and bankruptcy of small state-owned enterprises," Zhang said.

China has scored marked achievements in the management of state-owned assets since it set up an industry watchdog, the State Administration of State Property (SASP), in 1988, newspapers and the Xinhua news agency quoted Zhang as saying.
The SASP estimated the value of state-owned assets at more than 5.71 trillion yuan ($688 billion), at the end of 1995, said Zhang, who also heads the administration.
That included more than 4.5 trillion yuan in operational assets and over 1.2 trillion yuan in non-operational property.

State assets have increased steadily, and the growth rate was acclerating, Zhang said. He said the annual increase since 1949 has stood at 12.4 percent but jumped to 14.5 percent from 1980 and to 17.9 percent since 1990.
State property in enterprises accounts for more than 65 percent of total property of all China's enterprises.
Employees in state firms make up 67 percent of the total in urban areas, with 60 percent of state revenue coming from the state economy.
Of China's 302,000 state companies, large and medium-sized firms make up only 15.5 percent of the total, but their assets account for 82.3 percent of the total assets.
China was striving to curb the drain of state property. More than 300 cases of losses were investigated last year, helping to save 2.1 billion yuan in state assets, Zhang said.
Restructuring of the state sector was a major economic task for 1997, he said, referring to China's bid to get rid of loss-making industries and improve the more efficient ones.
"All areas must make a greater effort to liquidate existing assets," Zhang said.
"When setting up large enterprise groups or state-controlled companies, it is especially important to restructure and optimise the distribution of state-owned assets," said Zhang.
Proceeds from the transfer of state-owned property rights should be invested in industries that the state sees as in urgent need of development, he said.
